claims.text: The catalyst's enhanced ethanol-oxidation performance is governed by dynamic formation and regeneration of surface Pt–OH species.
The catalytically relevant Pt–OH species form at undercoordinated surface sites.
Ethanol oxidation proceeds through a bifunctional mechanism involving adjacent ethanol-adsorption and Pt–OH sites.
One surface site adsorbs and dehydrogenates ethanol.
Adjacent Pt–OH groups provide oxygen species that remove poisoning intermediates.
Removal of poisoning intermediates by Pt–OH increases activity.
Removal of poisoning intermediates by Pt–OH increases selectivity for complete ethanol oxidation.
Dynamic regeneration of Pt–OH and active sites improves catalyst durability.
The pristine nanoscale catalyst has abundant undercoordinated surface sites.
Mildly oxidative preconditioning promotes surface Pt–OH formation relative to reducing preconditioning.
Specific crystallographic facets participate in the Pt–OH-mediated bifunctional reaction steps.
Water activation under operating conditions forms Pt–OH groups.
Pt–OH reacts with adsorbed intermediates by donating oxygen and facilitates their complete oxidation to CO2.
Complete ethanol oxidation in the proposed cycle is a 12-electron and 12-proton process.
Oxidatively preconditioned catalysts will exhibit higher ethanol-oxidation current density than catalysts in which Pt–OH formation is suppressed.
Oxidatively preconditioned catalysts will produce more CO2 and fewer incomplete oxidation products.
Oxidatively preconditioned catalysts will have greater operational durability.
The proposed mechanism applies only in a potential window that permits both ethanol dehydrogenation and dynamic Pt–OH regeneration.
The proposed mechanism may fail when the surface is irreversibly poisoned or the potential lies outside the Pt–OH dynamic window.
